meta.documentTitle: Mahabharat Episode 4: Shakuntala and the Birth of Bharata

header.title: Mahabharat Episode 4: Shakuntala and the Birth of Bharata
header.description: Following the lineage of Puru (ancestor of the Pandavas and Kauravas) and Yadu (ancestor of the Yadavas), this story tells of Vishwamitra and Menaka, the birth and forest upbringing of Shakuntala, her fateful encounter with King Dushyanta, the curse of Sage Durvasa, and the rise of Emperor Bharata.

intro.title: The Birth of Shakuntala
leads: A few generations down from Puru lived King Vishwamitra, also known as Kaushika. Seeing the immense spiritual power of rishis and sages, he realized a king's power was tiny by comparison and resolved to become a sage himself.

He retreated into the forest and began performing intense austerities and sadhana. Observing Vishwamitra's fierce determination, Indra feared that if the king succeeded, his own celestial supremacy would be endangered.
To prevent this, Indra dispatched the apsara Menaka as a "honey-trap agent" to seduce Vishwamitra and disrupt his penance.

storyElements.html: Menaka succeeded in her mission and bore a baby girl. Upon realizing that he had lost all his hard-earned spiritual merit due to this distraction, Vishwamitra flew into a rage and abandoned both mother and child.

Being an apsara, Menaka was merely a visitor in this world with a "limited visa" and had to return to Devaloka. Since the father refused the child, Menaka left the baby on the banks of the river Malini before departing.
A flock of Shakun birds noticed the helpless infant, took a liking to her, and protected her from wild animals.

Sage Kanva happened to pass by and saw the unusual sight of birds guarding a human baby. He picked up the child, brought her to his ashram, and raised her as his daughter. Because she had been protected by Shakun birds, he named her Shakuntala. She grew up into a fine, compassionate young woman.

storyElements.text: King Dushyanta and the Wounded Stag

storyElements.html: One day, King Dushyanta was returning from a military campaign. Wanting to feed his army waiting at the edge of the forest, he went hunting and indiscriminately killed as many animals as he could.

He shot a large male stag with an arrow. Although his arrow struck true, the stag managed to flee. Dushyanta tracked the creature deep into the forest and found it in the hands of Shakuntala, who was nursing her pet stag with tender care.
Captivated by her grace and compassion, Dushyanta fell deeply in love with her. He stayed at the ashram and, with Sage Kanva's consent, married her.
As a token of remembrance and to seal their consummated marriage, Dushyanta slipped his official signet ring onto her finger—though it was oversized for her and did not fit properly.
After Dushyanta left, Shakuntala remained in a constant dream state—overwhelmed that a forest girl had suddenly become a queen and empress.

During this time, the quick-tempered Sage Durvasa visited Kanva's ashram. He spoke to Shakuntala, but she was so lost in thoughts of her husband that her eyes remained open without seeing him, and she failed to respond.
Feeling deeply insulted by her silence, Durvasa pronounced a harsh curse.

bubble.text: Whoever is holding your attention right now, may he forget you forever!
It cannot be! Why did you do this?

storyElements.html: The ashram residents intervened, explaining to Durvasa that Shakuntala was recently married to the king, was waiting for him, and was merely daydreaming. After receiving proper ashram hospitality, Durvasa calmed down and offered a remedy:

bubble.text: Yes, he has forgotten you, but the moment you show something that reminds him of you, he will remember.

storyElements.html: Shakuntala waited indefinitely, but Dushyanta never returned. In time, she gave birth to a son named Bharata.

As Bharata grew up in the forest, Sage Kanva told Shakuntala, "You should go and remind King Dushyanta that you are his wife, and that you have a son. It is not appropriate that a king’s son is growing up without being in touch with his father."

Shakuntala took young Bharata and journeyed toward the palace. While crossing a river in a boat, still lost in a dream of love, she put her hand into the water to feel it. Unnoticed by her, Dushyanta's oversized signet ring slipped off her finger and sank into the river.
Innocent of palace customs, Shakuntala entered the king's court to address Dushyanta.

bubble.text: Well, don’t you remember? I am your wife Shakuntala. This is your son.
How dare you! Who are you to even say such things?

storyElements.html: Wiped clean of his memory by Durvasa's curse, Dushyanta became furious and ousted her from the palace. Shakuntala was left heartbroken and bewildered, wondering how the man who loved her so intensely could completely erase her from his mind.

storyElements.text: The Rise of Bharata and Reunion

storyElements.html: Shaken by her painful first encounter with human society, Shakuntala retreated into the deep wilderness behind Kanva's ashram to raise her son.
Bharata grew up surrounded by wild animals—exceedingly brave, strong, and intimately connected to the natural world.
Years later, after Dushyanta recovered his lost ring, he happened to go hunting in that very forest. There, he stumbled upon a young boy fearlessly playing with full-grown lions and riding elephants.

bubble.text: Who are you? Are you some kind of superhuman being? Are you a god? Have you come from elsewhere?
No, I am Bharata, the son of Dushyanta.
I am Dushyanta. How come I don't know you?

storyElements.html: At that moment, Sage Kanva arrived and explained the entire tale of the marriage, the curse, and the lost ring. Realizing the truth, Dushyanta gladly welcomed Shakuntala and Bharata back to his palace.

Bharata grew to become an ideal human being and an extraordinary emperor celebrated for his immense wisdom, strength, and justice. It is after this great emperor that the nation was given the name Bharat or Bharatvarsh.
From the line of Emperor Bharata, the ancient history of the Lunar Dynasty continues down to the generations of the Kurus...
